g.text: Reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards (RLVR) has emerged
as a powerful paradigm for training large language models on tasks
g.title: N1 [Context] (cites=0) Reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards (RLVR) has emerged as a powerful paradigm for training large language models on tasks with automatic verification.

g.text: In code generation, unit tests provide a natural verifier: a solution is
correct if it passes all tests.
g.title: N2 [Context] (cites=0) In code generation, unit tests provide a natural verifier: a solution is correct if it passes all tests.

g.text: This approach has driven significant advances, from early work on
CodeRL (Le et al., 2022) and RLTF (Liu et al., 2023) to recent
breakthroughs like DeepSeek-R1 (DeepSeek-AI et al., 2025) and
g.title: N3 [Prior_Work] (cites=4) This approach has driven significant advances, from early work on CodeRL (Le et al., 2022) and RLTF (Liu et al., 2023) to recent breakthroughs like DeepSeek-R1 (DeepSeek-AI et al., 2025) and DeepSeekMath (Shao et al., 2024), which demonstrate that RL with verifiable rewards can substantially improve reasoning capabilities.

g.text: However, a fundamental challenge arises when computational
constraints limit the number of unit tests executed per rollout.
g.title: N4 [Context] (cites=0) However, a fundamental challenge arises when computational constraints limit the number of unit tests executed per rollout.

g.text: The standard approach uses the pass-rate—the fraction of tests
g.title: N5 [Prior_Work] (cites=0) The standard approach uses the pass-rate—the fraction of tests passed—as the reward signal.

g.text: Pass-rate has high variance at small m
When only m tests are executed (e.g., m = 5 for efficiency), this point
estimate has high variance and can mislead the policy.
g.title: N6 [Limitation] (cites=0) When only m tests are executed (e.g., m = 5 for efficiency), this point estimate has high variance and can mislead the policy.

g.text: A solution that passes 4 out of 5 tests might receive a reward of 0.8, yet
its true pass probability could plausibly range from 0.5 to 1.0.
g.title: N7 [Limitation] (cites=0) A solution that passes 4 out of 5 tests might receive a reward of 0.8, yet its true pass probability could plausibly range from 0.5 to 1.0.

g.text: This finite-sample noise creates a systematic failure mode: solutions that
happen to pass a favorable subset of tests receive inflated rewards,
potentially leading the policy to over-optimize noisy estimates rather than
g.title: N8 [Limitation] (cites=0) This finite-sample noise creates a systematic failure mode: solutions that happen to pass a favorable subset of tests receive inflated rewards, potentially leading the policy to over-optimize noisy estimates rather than true code quality.

g.text: We propose the Lower Confidence Bound (LCB) reward, which addresses this
g.title: N9 [Method] (cites=0) We propose the Lower Confidence Bound (LCB) reward, which addresses this challenge through principled uncertainty quantification.

g.text: Instead of treating the pass-rate as a point estimate, we model test
outcomes as Bernoulli trials with unknown success probability and place a
g.title: N10 [Method] (cites=0) Instead of treating the pass-rate as a point estimate, we model test outcomes as Bernoulli trials with unknown success probability and place a Beta prior over this probability.

g.text: δ-quantile of Beta posterior as reward
After observing npass successes out of m tests, we compute the δ-quantile of
the Beta posterior as the reward.
g.title: N11 [Method] (cites=0) After observing npass successes out of m tests, we compute the δ-quantile of the Beta posterior as the reward.

g.text: This provides a conservative estimate that naturally penalizes solutions
with high uncertainty: a solution passing 3/5 tests receives a lower LCB
reward than one passing 27/30 tests, even though both have the same
g.title: N12 [Method] (cites=0) This provides a conservative estimate that naturally penalizes solutions with high uncertainty: a solution passing 3/5 tests receives a lower LCB reward than one passing 27/30 tests, even though both have the same pass-rate of 0.6.

g.text: We propose the LCB reward for unit-test RLVR, which uses the lower
confidence bound of a Beta posterior to account for finite-sample
g.title: C1 [Contribution] (cites=0) We propose the LCB reward for unit-test RLVR, which uses the lower confidence bound of a Beta posterior to account for finite-sample uncertainty in pass-rate estimation.

g.text: We demonstrate that LCB (m=5) achieves state-of-the-art Pass@1
accuracy on MBPP+ (57.0%) and HumanEval+ (57.1%), outperforming
Pass-rate (2m=10) while using only half the verifier compute.
g.title: C2 [Contribution] (cites=0) We demonstrate that LCB (m=5) achieves state-of-the-art Pass@1 accuracy on MBPP+ (57.0%) and HumanEval+ (57.1%), outperforming Pass-rate (2m=10) while using only half the verifier compute.

g.text: We show that LCB is robust to hyperparameter choices (δ, prior)
and exhibits the most stable training dynamics among all tested
g.title: C3 [Contribution] (cites=0) We show that LCB is robust to hyperparameter choices (δ, prior) and exhibits the most stable training dynamics among all tested reward functions.
